1.q: קְרָ֤א בְ⁠גָרוֹן֙ אַל־תַּחְשֹׂ֔ךְ כַּ⁠שּׁוֹפָ֖ר הָרֵ֣ם קוֹלֶ֑⁠ךָ
1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Shout out loudly and without holding back, like a shofar]
This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

Here, **the throat** represents a loud, full voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Call out with a loud voice]

The words **you** and **your** and the implied “you” in the imperatives **Call out**, **Raise**, and **declare** are masculine singular because Yahweh is addressing Isaiah. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the masculine form if your language marks that distinction.

The point of this comparison is that just as **a shofar** produces a loud sound that can be heard from far away, so is **your voice** to be raised loudly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Raise your voice loudly, so that it can be heard from far away]

1.q: וְ⁠הַגֵּ֤ד לְ⁠עַמִּ⁠י֙ פִּשְׁעָ֔⁠ם וּ⁠לְ⁠בֵ֥ית יַעֲקֹ֖ב חַטֹּאתָֽ⁠ם
1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and declare to the descendants of Jacob how they are sinning against me]

In this verse, the word **my people** is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “my people.” Alternate translation: [to my people, all of them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they are rebelling against me]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to the house of Jacob declare their sins]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Jacob** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob. Alternate translation: [and to the descendants of Jacob]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sins**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they have sinned]

2.note: Yahweh is using **day, day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “every day” or “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [day after day]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people **seek** him physically, as one searches for something that is lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yet day after day they worship me]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his requirements for how people should live were **ways**, or paths, that a person could know and walk along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they delight in knowing how I want them to live]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a nation that has done righteousness** would sincerely seek to know its God’s will, so do these people outwardly appear to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [outwardly appearing to be a nation that does what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [has acted righteously]

This possessive form could describe: (1) the **approach of** the people to **God**. Alternate translation: [they delight in worshiping at the temple] or (2) the **approach of God** to the people. Alternate translation: [they believe that God will be pleased to draw near to them]

3.q: לָ֤⁠מָּה צַּ֨מְנוּ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א רָאִ֔יתָ עִנִּ֥ינוּ נַפְשֵׁ֖⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א & תֵדָ֑ע
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [Why have we fasted and humbled ourselves, but you have not noticed]

3.q: לָ֤⁠מָּה צַּ֨מְנוּ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א רָאִ֔יתָ עִנִּ֥ינוּ נַפְשֵׁ֖⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תֵדָ֑ע
3.note: The people are using the question form to complain that Yahweh has not noticed their fasting and self-denial. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We have fasted, but you have not seen; we have humbled our soul, but you have not known!]

3.q: לָ֤⁠מָּה צַּ֨מְנוּ֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א רָאִ֔יתָ עִנִּ֥ינוּ נַפְשֵׁ֖⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֣א תֵדָ֑ע
3.note: This is a quotation within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [They ask why they have fasted but I have not seen it, and why they have humbled themselves but I have not noticed]

The people are using **have we humbled our soul** as a common expression of the culture to mean “have we demonstrated our humility.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have we afflicted ourselves]

The people are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [why have we humbled our soul]

Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]
The words **you** and **your** are plural here and in verse 4 because Yahweh is addressing the Israelites, so use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

4.note: Isaiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

The terms **contention** and **quarrel** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for constant quarreling]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **contention** and **quarrel**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [so that you argue and fight]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **fist** that is characterized by **wickedness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and to strike with a wicked fist]
Here, **the height** represents “heaven,” where Yahweh lives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [up in heaven]

5.q: הֲ⁠כָ⁠זֶ֗ה יִֽהְיֶה֙ צ֣וֹם אֶבְחָרֵ֔⁠הוּ י֛וֹם עַנּ֥וֹת אָדָ֖ם נַפְשׁ֑⁠וֹ הֲ⁠לָ⁠כֹ֨ף כְּ⁠אַגְמֹ֜ן רֹאשׁ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠שַׂ֤ק וָ⁠אֵ֨פֶר֙ יַצִּ֔יעַ
5.note: Yahweh is using the question form to show that the outward fasting he describes is not the kind of fasting he desires. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The fast I choose is certainly not a day like this, a day in which a man outwardly models that he is humbling his soul by bowing his head like a reed and spreading sackcloth and ashes!]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people humbling their souls]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a reed** bends down low, so does a person bow **his head** in an outward show of humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [to bow his head low in humility, just as a reed bends down low]

Spreading out sackcloth and ashes to lie on was a symbolic action by which a person showed mourning or repentance. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and to lie down on sackcloth and ashes to show his remorse]

5.q: הֲ⁠לָ⁠זֶה֙ תִּקְרָא צ֔וֹם וְ⁠י֥וֹם רָצ֖וֹן לַ⁠יהוָֽה
5.note: Yahweh is using the question form to show that he does not accept this outward show of fasting as pleasing to him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is certainly not a day of fasting that is acceptable to Yahweh!]

The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the Israelites collectively as a nation. The words “you” and “your” are singular in verses 7–14 for the same reason. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **acceptance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and a day when Yahweh accepts people]

6.q: הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא זֶה֮ צ֣וֹם אֶבְחָרֵ⁠הוּ֒ פַּתֵּ֨חַ֙ חַרְצֻבּ֣וֹת רֶ֔שַׁע הַתֵּ֖ר אֲגֻדּ֣וֹת מוֹטָ֑ה וְ⁠שַׁלַּ֤ח רְצוּצִים֙ חָפְשִׁ֔ים וְ⁠כָל מוֹטָ֖ה תְּנַתֵּֽקוּ
6.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize what is involved in the kind of fasting he truly desires. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the ropes of the yoke, and to send the crushed ones free, and you shall break every yoke!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the oppression that wicked people impose on others were **bonds** that tie up their victims. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the restraints with which people wickedly hold others down]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if oppression were a **yoke** that people are forced to wear, like an animal harnessed for heavy work. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what oppresses people]

The expression **the crushed ones** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language, stating who does the action, namely, those who oppress these people. Alternate translation: [the ones whom others crush]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people who are oppressed had been physically **crushed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the oppressed people]
The word **you** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the Israelites as a group, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

7.q: הֲ⁠ל֨וֹא פָרֹ֤ס לָֽ⁠רָעֵב֙ לַחְמֶ֔⁠ךָ וַ⁠עֲנִיִּ֥ים מְרוּדִ֖ים תָּ֣בִיא בָ֑יִת
7.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that true fasting involves sharing food with the hungry and caring for the poor. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should divide your bread with the hungry, and you shall bring the wandering poor into your house!]

Yahweh is using **your bread**, one kind of food, to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own food]

Yahweh is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to those who are hungry]

Yahweh is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and you shall bring the poor people who are wandering]

Yahweh is using the adjective **naked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a naked person]

Yahweh is using **hide yourself from your flesh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “ignore the needs of your own relatives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall not ignore the needs of your own relatives]

Yahweh is using **your flesh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “your own relatives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall not hide yourself from your own relatives]

8.note: Here, **Then** introduces the result of a condition: Yahweh will bring these blessings only if the people practice the kind of fasting he has described. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [If you do these things, then]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s deliverance and wellbeing were **light** that could **break forth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your wellbeing will burst into view]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the dawn** breaks suddenly and grows steadily brighter, so will the people’s wellbeing appear and increase. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [suddenly and steadily, like the light at dawn]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s **healing** were a plant that could **sprout up** quickly from the ground. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will quickly grow strong]

Yahweh is speaking of **your righteousness** as if it were a living thing that could walk in front of you, like a guard leading the way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And your righteousness will protect you as you go forward]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the righteous things you do]
Here, **to your face** represents “in front of you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of you]

Yahweh is speaking of **the glory of Yahweh** as if it were a living thing that could gather you up and guard you from behind. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [glorious Yahweh will protect you from behind]

9.note: This is a quotation within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and he will tell you that he is here to help]

Yahweh is using **Behold me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Here I am, ready to help you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Here I am, ready to help you]

Yahweh is using **the putting forth of the finger** as a common expression of the culture to mean “falsely accusing or scorning people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the making of false accusations against people]

10.note: Here, **your soul** represents yourself and your own resources that you give to others. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and you give of yourself to the hungry]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if prosperity were **light** and adversity were **darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then you will begin to prosper in the midst of your adversity]

The point of this comparison is that just as **noon** is the brightest time of day, so will the people’s **gloom** become bright. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and your gloom will become as bright as noon] or [and your gloom will be no more]

11.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if times of hardship were **dry places** where there is no water. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will provide for you in times of hardship]

Yahweh is using **your bones**, one part of the body, to represent the whole person and their health. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will make your whole body strong]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a watered garden** and **a spring of water** always have plenty of water and flourish, so will the person whom Yahweh blesses continually flourish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [always flourishing like a well-watered garden and an ever-flowing spring]

12.note: Yahweh is using **the desolations of eternity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “ruins that have lain waste for a very long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the places that have been in ruins for a very long time]

Yahweh is using **generation and generation** as a common expression of the culture to mean “many ages long ago.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the foundations laid many ages ago]

12.q: וְ⁠קֹרָ֤א לְ⁠ךָ֙ גֹּדֵ֣ר פֶּ֔רֶץ מְשֹׁבֵ֥ב נְתִיב֖וֹת לָ⁠שָֽׁבֶת
12.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people who rebuild the ruined city as if they were a **Repairer of the Breach** and a **Restorer of Streets to Dwell In**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and one will call you the person who repairs broken walls, the person who restores streets for people to live in]

The pronoun **one** does not refer to any specific person; it refers to people in general. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers, for example by using a passive form such as “you will be called.” Alternate translation: [and you will be called] or [and people will call you]

13.note: Yahweh is using **turn back your foot from the Sabbath** as a common expression of the culture to mean “stop pursuing your own interests on the Sabbath.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you stop pursuing your own interests on the Sabbath]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pleasures**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what pleases you]

The expression **honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [honoring Yahweh as holy]
This could mean: (1) speaking idle or useless words. Alternate translation: [and speaking idle words] or (2) making business deals. Alternate translation: [and making business deals]

14.q: וְ⁠הִרְכַּבְתִּ֖י⁠ךָ עַל־בָּ֣מֳותֵי אָ֑רֶץ וְ⁠הַאֲכַלְתִּ֗י⁠ךָ נַחֲלַת֙ יַעֲקֹ֣ב אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ
14.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I will make you greatly prosperous, giving you the blessing that I promised to your ancestor Jacob]

Yahweh is using **make you ride on the heights of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “give you victory and prosperity.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will give you victory and prosperity]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would **feed** the people with the land that they inherit. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will give you the inheritance of Jacob your father]
Yahweh is using the term **father** to mean “ancestor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Jacob your ancestor]

Isaiah is using **the mouth of Yahweh**, one part of Yahweh, to represent Yahweh himself, who has spoken. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has spoken]
